blocks.text: The Sedona Method of Emotional Release

inline.s: Watch your thoughts, feel your emotions, and observe your reactions to events.
Your browser does not support the video tag.

The Sedona Method of Emotional Release is a set of methods that can resolve inner conditions from the very shallow to the very deep — usable anytime and anywhere, simple and extremely effective. The objects of release are negative emotions, cravings for harmful habits, and so on. Each release makes you lighter and happier; and if you keep releasing, you will become lighter and happier still.
The premise of this releasing method is that the essential nature of every person is an infinite existence of joy, omniscience, and omnipotence (
being
, also called the fundamental essence). Only because of the habits, fixed views, complexes,
delusions
and other such mental disturbances accumulated in the present consciousness, do we fail to perceive it. Conversely, if these accumulated burdens are cleared away, the essence of existence (
being
) will naturally reveal itself; and in the process of progress, one also becomes lighter and happier as the burdens are removed.

Its main logic is this: apart from the two ways of suppressing and exploding (or being overwhelmed), every person is born with the capacity to release emotions, but this releasing capacity has been gradually forgotten through long-term social conditioning. Yet through conscious awareness, this capacity can be immediately recovered. Moreover, because the mechanism used by this method is in fact innate, the capacity to operate it can be recovered by everyone, and the method of operation is very direct and simple.
Because the outward expression of these mental disturbances is emotion, including psychogenic reactions; and their inner source of motive force is the self (
Ego
)'s ingrained reactions. Therefore the Sedona Method's angles of releasing are of two kinds: one focused on the emotion, and one focused on the inner motive force.
[Psychogenic] Originating from inferior psychological stimuli in social activity and mental life.
The following is a brief introduction to this releasing method.
The Sedona Method has four ways of releasing in all: direct releasing, diving into the core, holistic releasing, and allowing to surface.

These four ways produce the same result, but because they differ in how easy they are to grasp and follow, the Sedona Method mainly uses two of them: allowing to surface and holistic releasing (the latter less often).

Direct releasing means simply throwing the emotion behind you, an instinct that even animals possess. But “throwing it behind you” does not mean suppressing it; rather, it is like hearing a joke — after two bursts of laughter it vanishes into thin air. That is, you have no intention of keeping it in your mind.
On this point, Hale liked to use the “pencil experiment” in every seminar to illustrate the crux of the matter:

Now please take out a small object, such as a pencil, and place it on your hand. In this experiment we liken the pencil to your emotion and the hand to your awareness. Now grasp the pencil with your hand and begin to squeeze — squeeze hard, with all your might. Don't you feel quite uncomfortable? If you keep holding without letting go, it will feel even more uncomfortable.

Good. Now please open your hand and let the pencil roll on your palm. We all know the pencil is not stuck to the hand, right? So the reason it stayed in our hand just now is that we ourselves were holding on to it. Likewise, our relation to our emotions is just like the relation between the palm and the pencil. In life, when we notice we have unpleasant feelings or emotions, we assume the emotions and feelings are troubling us, and unconsciously we cling to them and won't let go.

Moreover, most of us unconsciously merge ourselves with our emotions — that is, we fail to view them objectively, and take the emotion to be an inseparable part of ourselves. This is the same principle as your just now gripping the pencil and not letting go. Thus when we have unpleasant emotions, we likewise believe we are entangled by them (when the fact is that we ourselves are holding on to the emotion).

Now please open your hand, palm facing down. And then? The pencil drops all by itself! Isn't that easy? This is the “direct releasing” of the Sedona Method! Whenever you feel you have unpleasant emotions, you can simply let them go directly.
In fact, we have the power to control our emotions at any time and any place; we simply do not know it!

This sounds simple, but for one who has never experienced the feeling of “releasing,” direct releasing would likely prove quite elusive. So in the courses, the methods mainly used are the others, which are easier to grasp.

blocks.text: 2. Diving into the Core (Diving into the Core of the Emotion)

inline.s: Diving into the core means that whatever emotion you have, and however great its intensity, as long as you look earnestly into the depths of your inner mind, you will find that there is nothing there — it is empty and calm. Thus you can perceive that the so-called emotion is merely a three-foot wave on the surface of the sea, while beneath it remains a sheet of stillness. Then, by contrast, the emotion will vanish of itself with a “pop,” like a soap bubble.

The idea of holistic releasing lies in this: the world we inhabit is a relative world, where whatever comes also goes, and whatever has a front has a back. Yet it is also a world of wholes, where everything is like a coin or a sheet of paper — you cannot draw out only the front without also drawing out the back. Emotions are the same: when there is an emotion of being persecuted, hidden behind it there must also be an emotion of persecuting. Thus the Sedona Method makes use of this relation: when an emotion cannot be pulled out, it works back and forth between the front and the back to pull it out. This is what holistic releasing means.

blocks.text: 4. Allowing to Surface (Welcoming or Allowing the Emotion)

inline.s: This is the easiest to follow and easiest to master method in Sedona, and also its principal releasing technique. Its concept is that emotion by nature seeks an outlet; as long as we use our attention to raise it from the subconscious to the surface consciousness, and allow it to exist, it will disappear of itself without a trace, like a balloon whose mouth has been opened.
Of course, if your emotion is at the very moment of flaring up, then you need not raise it any further — it is already in the surface consciousness.

blocks.text: 2. The Steps of Releasing and the Prompting Questions

inline.s: In Sedona, releasing is divided into six steps, used together with five prompting questions. The objects of releasing are negative emotions, cravings for harmful habits, and so on. These five prompting questions are:
1. What are you feeling inside right now?
2. Can you allow this feeling to surface?
3. Can you let it go?
4. Are you willing to let it go?
5. When?

When operating and posing the questions, one may take the first-person perspective or the third-person perspective — in short, whichever works better. At the same time, it is fine to do it with eyes open or closed.
The following are the six steps of the operation:
Step One:
When an emotion appears (or after recalling the event you wish to release), place your attention on the emotion that has surfaced, and ask yourself:
What are you feeling inside right now?

This feeling need not be particularly strong; especially when first learning, one often cannot stir up anything in the heart at all. But even a blank is fine — in fact, blankness itself is also a mental image, so simply continue.
However, the emphasis of this step is on the feeling “now.” The release of emotion must begin from the feeling presently present, even if it is a blank or a bewilderment.
Step Two:

Allow (or welcome) the surfacing of this feeling, including the images (or pictures), sounds (or words), and sensations (or actions) that come with it. Allow as much as possible the condition you are now experiencing, and ask yourself:
Can you allow this feeling to surface?

This step is the crux of the whole releasing method. The reason our emotions are repeatedly triggered is generally that they have not been given the space to exist naturally, so that this negative energy keeps searching for an outlet.

Our usual ways of handling emotion are none other than suppression and explosion (or being overwhelmed). Of these, suppression is easier to understand: forcing oneself to push it down, or simply looking away and pretending it does not exist.

But what is the difference between explosion and allowing to surface? In fact, the difference between them lies only in whether we “throw ourselves into” it — that is, whether we maintain the distinction between self and other. We are the “self,” and the emotion is the “other.”

To put it simply, view the emotion like a neighbor's dog climbing onto us and licking here and there. Although it is happening on our body, it is, after all, someone else's dog, and you do not take it for “your own” dog.
This is also the reason it is suggested to release in the third person.
Moreover, when the emotion surfaces, there is no need to attach any label to it; direct cognition is enough. Labeling, on the contrary, tends to distract the mind.
Step Three:
Ask yourself:
Can you let it go?

The emphasis of all the prompting questions posed in the releasing process is not on their literal meaning but on the “prompting.” So in answering, there is no need to think or deliberate; simply look at the first response of your own heart, and whether the answer is “yes” or “no,” it will not hinder the releasing.
So whatever the answer, please continue to the next step.
Step Four:
Ask yourself:
Are you willing to let it go?
As before, whatever the answer, please continue to the next step.
Step Five:
Ask yourself:
When will you let it go?
This is merely prompting you that you can let go “now” — but in fact you can decide to let go at any time.
Step Six:
Repeat the operation of the first five steps until you feel that the emotion no longer continues to gnaw at you.

If you find a particular emotion especially hard to release, the corresponding strategy is simply to allow it to surface or exist. In fact, often once it is thus set aside, it will disappear of itself, for no apparent reason.

Moreover, for beginners, if a guided recording can be used to assist during practice, the effect will be more ideal. For one thing, it saves mental effort and reduces distraction, and at the same time lets one know the approximate rhythm of releasing.

Also, experience shows that once you are familiar with the feeling of releasing, you need only allow it to surface — no other steps are needed. Once it has surfaced completely, it will release itself, without even the prompting questions. Everyone may try this.
